vllm: Which problem does PagedAttention mainly solve in vLLM?
Fragmentation and waste of KV cache memory
Slow tokenization of very long prompts
Overflow of FP16 values inside softmax
Load imbalance across data loader workers
PagedAttention stores the KV cache in small blocks allocated on demand, so memory is not reserved for the maximum length and fragmentation stays low.
In vLLM's PagedAttention, how is the KV cache of one sequence stored?
In fixed-size blocks that need not be contiguous
In one contiguous buffer sized for the max length
In CPU memory, copied to the GPU every step
In a compressed form decoded on every attention call
A block table maps each sequence's logical blocks to physical blocks anywhere in GPU memory, much like page tables map virtual pages.
The design of PagedAttention in vLLM is inspired by which operating system concept?
Virtual memory and paging
Round-robin process scheduling
File system journaling
Hardware interrupt handling
Blocks act like pages and sequences act like processes, with a block table translating logical to physical locations.
vLLM generates 4 samples for the same prompt (parallel sampling). How does PagedAttention save memory here?
The samples share the prompt's KV blocks, with copy-on-write on divergence
Each sample recomputes the prompt with a smaller batch
Samples run one after another and the cache is cleared between them
The prompt is kept on CPU and streamed to each sample
Physical blocks are reference-counted, so the prompt is stored once; a block is copied only when a sample needs to write a different token into it.
What does continuous (iteration-level) batching in vLLM do differently from static batching?
Adds and removes requests at every decoding step
Pads all requests to one length before the batch starts
Serves one request at a time to minimize latency
Groups only requests with identical prompt lengths
The scheduler runs per iteration, so finished requests leave and queued ones join without waiting for the whole batch to complete.
Why does continuous batching raise throughput when serving LLMs?
Finished short requests free their slot instead of idling
It loads fewer model parameters for each request
It skips attention over padding tokens in the encoder
It caches final answers for repeated prompts
With static batching the GPU waits for the longest request; continuous batching refills freed slots right away, keeping the GPU busy.
Which vLLM engine argument caps how many sequences are processed in a single scheduler iteration?
--max-num-seqs
--max-model-len
--block-size
--swap-space

Which option makes vllm serve shard a model across 4 GPUs with tensor parallelism?
--tensor-parallel-size 4
--pipeline-parallel-size 4
--num-gpus-per-model 4
--num-shards 4
--tensor-parallel-size splits each layer across GPUs; --pipeline-parallel-size would split by layers instead.
When serving a model with tensor parallelism in vLLM, which model property must generally be divisible by the tensor parallel size?
The number of attention heads
The number of transformer layers
The maximum context length
The number of tokens in a prompt
Tensor parallelism gives each GPU a subset of attention heads, so the head count must split evenly across ranks.
What does tensor parallelism split across GPUs in vLLM?
The weight matrices inside each layer
Whole layers, a consecutive group per GPU
Separate requests, each on a full model copy
The tokenizer and detokenizer stages
Each GPU holds a slice of every layer's weights and partial results are combined with all-reduce; splitting whole layers is pipeline parallelism.
A model is launched with vllm serve ... --tensor-parallel-size 2 --pipeline-parallel-size 2. How many GPUs does it use?
The total is the product of the two sizes: 2 tensor-parallel ranks in each of 2 pipeline stages.
What does --gpu-memory-utilization 0.9 control in vLLM?
The share of GPU memory vLLM may use in total
The share of GPU cores reserved for vLLM
The share of memory left for other processes
The batch size as a share of --max-num-seqs
vLLM uses up to that fraction of GPU memory for weights, activations and KV cache, and turns the remainder after weights into KV cache blocks.
vLLM fails at startup: the model's max sequence length is larger than the KV cache can hold. Which change directly fixes this?
Lower --max-model-len
Raise --max-num-seqs
Raise --block-size to 128
Disable the tokenizer cache
A smaller max length means one sequence needs fewer KV blocks; raising --gpu-memory-utilization would also help, but more sequences or bigger blocks would not.
What does automatic prefix caching (--enable-prefix-caching) do in vLLM?
Reuses KV blocks of a shared prompt prefix
Stores finished responses keyed by prompt
Caches tokenizer outputs on the local disk
Precompiles CUDA graphs for batch sizes
Requests that start with the same tokens, such as a shared system prompt, can reuse already computed KV blocks and skip that prefill work.
In vLLM, what happens to running sequences when the KV cache has no free blocks left?
Some are preempted and resumed later
The server crashes with an OOM error
New tokens overwrite other sequences' blocks
Generation silently continues on the CPU
The scheduler preempts lower-priority sequences, freeing their blocks, and later restores them by recomputation (or swapping in older versions).
Which vLLM option stores the KV cache in a lower precision to fit more tokens in GPU memory?
--kv-cache-dtype fp8
--kv-cache-dtype fp64
--dtype int64
--quantization none

In TGI, what does --max-total-tokens limit?
Input plus generated tokens of one request
Tokens across all requests in a batch
Tokens generated per second by the whole server
Tokens held in the prefix cache at once
It is a per-request ceiling on prompt length plus new tokens, which sets the memory budget each client can use.
With continuous batching in TGI, when can a new request start being processed?
Between decoding steps, while others still run
Only after the whole current batch finishes
Only when the queue is full to batch size
Only after the server rebuilds its batches
The router adds waiting requests to the running batch at step boundaries, so short and long requests overlap.
TGI is at its --max-concurrent-requests limit and another request arrives. What does the client get?
An HTTP 429 overloaded error
An HTTP 404 not found error
A response with empty text
A silent wait with no limit

What does FlashAttention speed up in TGI?
Attention, by tiling to cut memory traffic
Tokenization, by caching vocabulary lookups
Weight loading, by compressing files
Token streaming, by batching events
FlashAttention computes attention in tiles kept in fast on-chip memory, reducing reads and writes to GPU high-bandwidth memory.
Does FlashAttention change the attention result compared with standard attention?
No, it computes exact attention
Yes, it uses a low-rank approximation
Yes, it removes softmax normalization
Yes, it limits attention to a window

How does FlashAttention's extra memory for attention scale with sequence length N?
Linearly, as the N x N matrix is never stored
Quadratically, just like standard attention does
Cubically, because of the tiling overhead
It stays constant for any sequence length N
Scores are computed tile by tile and never materialized as a full N x N matrix, so memory grows linearly instead of quadratically.

Less memory, with some possible quality loss
More accuracy, but much higher memory use
Faster training, but no inference support
Larger vocabulary, but more latency per token

Why do chat interfaces stream tokens from TGI instead of waiting for the full answer?

Streaming lowers total GPU compute per request
Streaming makes the output deterministic

The finished request keeps generating padding tokens
Finished requests are removed right away, so the GPU keeps working on a full batch.
How does the paged KV cache in TensorRT-LLM store keys and values?
In fixed-size blocks allocated on demand
In one buffer sized for the max length
In CPU memory, copied for every token
In a single shared block for all requests

What does KV cache reuse in TensorRT-LLM help with?
Requests that share a prefix, like a system prompt
Requests that each need a different model loaded
Prompts that are shorter than a single cache block
Batches that contain only one request at a time
Blocks computed for a common prefix are kept and reused, skipping repeated prefill work.
Why store the KV cache in FP8 or INT8 instead of FP16?
It halves KV memory, so more tokens fit
It doubles the model's context length limit
It makes attention exact in all cases
It removes the need for any prefill
Each cached value takes one byte instead of two, allowing larger batches or longer contexts, with a small accuracy risk.
How does KV cache memory grow during LLM serving?
Linearly with sequence length and batch size
Quadratically with the size of the vocabulary
Only with the number of model weights
It stays fixed once the model loads
Each token of each sequence stores keys and values for every layer, so memory is proportional to tokens times batch.
Why do grouped-query attention (GQA) models need a smaller KV cache?
Several query heads share one key/value head
They store keys but never store values
They use a smaller vocabulary than MHA
They cache only the final layer's output vectors
With fewer KV heads than query heads, fewer keys and values are stored per token.
In TensorRT-LLM's KvCacheConfig, what does free_gpu_memory_fraction set?
Share of free memory after loading used for KV cache
Share of the model weights offloaded to CPU memory at load
Share of incoming requests rejected when busy
Share of GPU cores held back for attention
After the model loads, this fraction of the remaining free GPU memory is allocated to the KV cache pool.
A 70B model does not fit on one GPU. For the lowest per-token latency on 8 NVLink GPUs in one node, which setup is usually best?
Tensor parallelism across all 8 GPUs
Pipeline parallelism with 8 stages
Eight data-parallel model copies
CPU offload of half of the layers

Which command launches TensorRT-LLM's OpenAI-compatible HTTP server in recent releases?
trtllm-serve
trtllm-api
trtllm-host
trt-openai

The world size is the product of tensor and pipeline parallel sizes: 4 x 2 = 8.
Which NVIDIA library provides the multi-GPU collective communication that TensorRT-LLM model parallelism uses?
NCCL
cuDNN
cuBLAS
nvJPEG
NCCL implements all-reduce and other collectives over NVLink and networks; cuBLAS and cuDNN are compute libraries.
How does the context (prefill) phase differ from the generation phase in LLM inference?
Prefill handles all prompt tokens in one pass
Prefill generates one new token per step
Prefill runs only on the CPU, not the GPU
Prefill skips all of the attention layers in the model

Why is the generation (decode) phase of LLM inference usually memory-bandwidth bound?
Each step reads all weights for one token per sequence
Each step trains the weights a little more on new data
Each step reloads the tokenizer files from disk again
Each step sorts the entire vocabulary by probability
Little math is done per byte of weights loaded, so memory bandwidth, not compute, limits decoding speed.
Why does weight-only INT4 quantization (such as AWQ) speed up decoding in TensorRT-LLM?
Less weight data is read from memory per step
Activations are cut to 4 bits for all of the compute
The model needs fewer transformer layers
Attention is skipped for repeated tokens
Decoding is bandwidth bound, so shrinking weights to 4 bits cuts the bytes read for each generated token.

A cheap draft proposes tokens; the target verifies them
Two separate models vote on every token that they generate
The model skips several layers for the easy tokens
The server guesses incoming prompts before they arrive
Verifying several drafted tokens in one target forward pass can produce multiple tokens per step.
Does standard speculative decoding with rejection sampling change the output distribution of the target model?
No, it matches the target model
Yes, it follows the draft model
Yes, it averages both models
Yes, it removes all randomness
The acceptance rule guarantees that outputs follow the target model's distribution; only speed changes.
What is Medusa, one of the speculative decoding methods supported by TensorRT-LLM?
Extra heads on the model predict future tokens
A separate large model that checks safety
A cache that stores whole past answers
A tokenizer that merges frequent words
Medusa adds decoding heads that guess several next tokens, which the base model then verifies, so no separate draft model is needed.
When does speculative decoding give little or no speedup?
When most draft tokens are rejected
When the target model is very large
When the GPU has plenty of free memory
When prompts are short and simple
A low acceptance rate means the extra draft work rarely saves target model steps.

Your Docker Hub username and its account password

A dataset manifest that lists the audio file paths
A compiled TensorRT engine for GPUs
A log file written during training

A tokenizer and a language model
An ASR model and a punctuation model
A speaker ID model and a denoiser

@vectorize

When does Numba compile a function decorated with @njit and no signature?
On its first call, for the argument types used
When the module that defines it is first imported
When the package is installed with pip
Before every single call to the function

A second version is compiled for float64
The float is silently cast to int64 and reused
The second call raises a TypeError
Both calls run in pure Python

Calling a pandas DataFrame method
Looping over the elements of a NumPy array
Calling math.sqrt on a float
Creating an array with np.zeros

What does cache=True do in @njit(cache=True)?
Saves compiled code to disk for later runs
Caches return values for repeated inputs
Keeps arrays in the GPU memory cache
Stores the source code in memory

The first call includes compile time
The first call runs on the GPU
The second call uses more CPU threads
The first call skips all loops

Runs loop iterations across threads
Runs the loop on the GPU instead
Unrolls the whole loop at compile time
Reverses the loop's iteration order

It behaves like an ordinary range
It raises a compile-time typing error
It launches threads anyway
It moves the loop to a GPU

Treats it as a reduction and combines it safely

Keeps only the last thread's value for s
Runs that loop serially without any notice

Every iteration doing out[0] += a[i]

Mark the array as global inside the loop

np.empty returns a Python list instead of an array
